steps.body: You now own three lenses, and a real description uses **all of them**. Minutes to get to school: 5, 10, 10, 15, 15, 15, 20, 20, 25. **Shape:** one peak at 15, symmetric. **Center:** median 15 (the mean is 15 too — symmetric data agrees with itself). **Spread:** range 25 − 5 = 20, IQR 20 − 10 = 10. One plot, three questions, one honest paragraph.

widget.prompt: Build the box plot: minimum 2, Q1 6, median 10, Q3 14, maximum 18.
widget.successFeedback: The box holds the middle half of the data and the whiskers hold the rest. A box plot throws away every individual value and keeps only the five that describe the spread — which is exactly why it is so good at comparing groups.
widget.orderFeedback: The five markers must be in order: min ≤ Q1 ≤ median ≤ Q3 ≤ max.
widget.valueFeedback: The markers are in order but not on the right values. Read the five numbers again.

predict.prompt: Whiskers reach the min and max. Will the LEFT whisker (2 to 6) be shorter or longer than the box (6 to 14)?
predict.reveal: The left whisker spans 4 while the box spans 8 — the lowest quarter of this data huddles close, and the plot's shape says so at a glance.

cml.actionGoal: Construct a five-number summary and coordinate ordered data with center and spread.

explanationVariants: The median 15 steps aside (odd count); lower half 5, 10, 10, 15 gives Q1 = 10, upper half 15, 20, 20, 25 gives Q3 = 20; IQR = 20 − 10 = 10.
The middle half of the trips runs from 10 to 20 minutes — a band 10 wide.

widget.prompt: Same trip data. Q1 = 10 and Q3 = 20. What is the IQR?

commonErrors.feedback: 30 adds the quartiles (20 + 10). The IQR is the width between them: 20 − 10 = 10.
20 is the RANGE (25 − 5) — endpoints, not fences. IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 20 − 10 = 10.

hints: Which two numbers feed an IQR?

steps.body: Assemble it **in context, with units**: 'Trips to school center around **15 minutes** (median), with the middle half between 10 and 20 (**IQR 10**); the shape is **symmetric** with a single peak at 15 and no outliers.' Notice what's missing from bad descriptions: a bare '15' answers nothing — fifteen *what*, of *what data*, how *spread out*?

widget.prompt: A student describes the trip data. Drag each fragment to the lens it uses.

items.label: "one symmetric peak at 15"
items.feedback: Peaks, symmetry, gaps, and outliers are the plot's SHAPE — how the dots arrange themselves.

items.label: "a typical trip is about 15 minutes"
items.feedback: 'Typical' is a CENTER claim — it locates the middle of the data.

items.label: "the middle half spans 10 minutes"
items.feedback: A span is a width — that's the IQR talking, a SPREAD lens.

items.label: "trips stretch from 5 to 25 minutes"
items.feedback: Min-to-max stretch is the range — SPREAD, not a location or a shape.

widget.missFeedback: Ask what the fragment answers: how the dots are arranged (shape), where the middle sits (center), or how wide the data runs (spread).
widget.successFeedback: Tagged — a full description hits all three lenses at least once.

explanationVariants: 'The average is 15' gives one center — no spread, no shape, no units or context. The full report pairs a center with a spread and names the shape.
One lens out of three: a reader can't tell whether trips vary by minutes or by an hour.

widget.prompt: Which report of the trip data is INCOMPLETE as a description of the distribution?

options.label: "The average is 15."
options.feedback: Right — it's a lone center with no units, no spread, no shape. True, but not a description.

options.label: "Trips center near 15 minutes, middle half 10–20, symmetric, no outliers."
options.feedback: That one's complete — center (15), spread (IQR band), and shape (symmetric, no outliers) all present. The bare 'average is 15' is the incomplete one.

options.label: "Median 15 min; IQR 10 min; single symmetric peak."
options.feedback: Compact but complete — one center, one spread, and the shape. The lone '15' report is the one that leaves the reader guessing.

hints: Count the lenses in each report.
Shape, center, spread — a full report touches all three.
One report has just a single center.

explanationVariants: Symmetric data balances, so the level-out point (mean) lands on the middle position (median): both are 15 here. Big mean–median gaps appear only when data is lopsided.
The sum is 135 across 9 trips: mean 135 ÷ 9 = 15 — exactly the median, as symmetry predicts.

widget.prompt: The trip data sums to 135 across 9 trips. Compute the MEAN — and notice how it compares to the median of 15.

commonErrors.feedback: 135 is the sum; divide by the 9 trips: 135 ÷ 9 = 15 — landing exactly on the median, as symmetric data does.
That's 135 ÷ 8 — there are NINE trips. 135 ÷ 9 = 15, matching the median.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 135 ÷ 9 = 15. Mean equals median — the signature of symmetric data.

hints: It should land on the median.

explanationVariants: Option (a) is the only report with all three lenses in context: shape (symmetric peak), center (median 15 minutes), spread (IQR 10). The others repeat one lens or drop the units.
Check each candidate against the checklist — shape? center? spread? units? Only one passes all four.

widget.prompt: Pick the BEST one-sentence description of the trip data.

options.label: "Trips cluster symmetrically around a median of 15 minutes, with the middle half spanning just 10 minutes."
options.feedback: Shape, center, spread, units, context — the complete picture in one sentence.

options.label: "The mean is 15 and the median is 15."
options.feedback: Two CENTERS is still one lens. Trade one for a spread and add the shape: 'symmetric around 15 minutes, IQR 10.'

options.label: "The range is 20 and the IQR is 10."
options.feedback: Two SPREADS with no center or shape — how wide, but around what, arranged how? Anchor it: median 15 minutes, symmetric.

hints: A complete report touches shape, center, AND spread.
Two centers — or two spreads — still cover only one lens.
Only one option names all three.

takeaways: Describe a distribution with shape + center + spread, in context and with units.
Symmetric data: mean ≈ median (here both 15), and either center serves.
A single number — however correct — is not a description.
steps.teaser: next: when the data is lopsided, which center and which spread deserve the job?

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Three lenses:** SHAPE is how the dots arrange (peaks, symmetry, outliers); CENTER is where the middle sits (mean or median); SPREAD is how wide the data runs (range or IQR). A full description uses one of each.

explanationVariants: 'Spans 10 minutes' is a width — spread. Shape describes arrangement; center describes location.
Widths and stretches are always the spread lens.

widget.prompt: "The middle half spans 10 minutes" — which lens is that?

options.label: Spread
options.feedback: Yes — a span is a width, and widths are spread (this one is the IQR).

options.label: Center
options.feedback: A center would LOCATE the middle (like 'median 15'). 'Spans 10' measures a width — that's spread.

options.label: Shape
options.feedback: Shape talks arrangement — peaks, symmetry, outliers. A 10-minute span is a width: spread.
